title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement: There are piles of bananas and h hours. Each hour Koko picks one pile and eats up to k bananas from it; leftovers in that pile wait, and she never switches piles mid-hour. Find the smallest whole speed k that finishes every pile within h hours.

example.caption: At speed 3 the piles need 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 hours, too many. At speed 4 they need 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours. So 4 is the answer.

idea.sentence: Do not search the piles, search the speeds. A speed is either too slow or fast enough, and that answer never flips back as speed grows.

jargon.plain: Instead of looking for a value inside an array, look for the best number in a range, and use a yes/no check to decide which half to drop.
Only changes one way. If speed 5 is fast enough, so is every speed above 5.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the piles and the hours, e.g. [3,6,7,11] and 8. Keep piles small so the speed line stays readable.

rows.name: Try every speed
rows.note: Up to m speeds, and each check walks all n piles.

rows.name: Binary search on speed
rows.note: About log m speeds are checked, each in one pass over the piles.

fast.takeaway: The check is a plain loop. Binary search only decides which speed to check next, and that cuts m tries down to log m.

stages.title: Speed range
stages.note: Speeds run from 1 to the biggest pile. The biggest pile always works, so it is the first best.

stages.title: Try a middle speed
stages.note: While some speeds are undecided, pick the middle one.

stages.title: Count the hours
stages.note: Each pile takes ceil(pile / speed) hours. Add them up.

stages.title: Keep or raise
stages.note: Within h hours: save it and try slower, r = m - 1. Over h: too slow, so l = m + 1.

stages.title: Answer
stages.note: When the range is empty, best holds the slowest speed that still finishes in time.

edges.title: Hours equal piles
edges.why: One hour per pile means she must finish the biggest pile in one hour. That is the top of the range.

edges.title: Lots of time
edges.why: Speed 1 already works, so the search must be able to settle on the very bottom of the range.

edges.title: Single pile
edges.why: At speed 3 the pile needs 4 hours. At speed 4 it needs 3. Rounding up is what makes 4 the answer.

edges.title: Huge pile
edges.why: Speeds go up to a billion, but only about 30 are tested. The hour total can also get large with many piles.

gotchas.text: Math.ceil(p / m) is right. Math.floor(p / m) or integer-style division drops the leftover bananas and under-counts the hours.
Math.max(...piles) pushes every pile onto the call stack. It is fine for the usual limits, but a huge array can throw a RangeError. A reduce loop has no such limit.
Ceiling division on ints is (p + m - 1) / m. Dividing floats just to call math.Ceil is slower and can round wrongly for large values.
The hour total can reach about 10^13 with many big piles. That fits in Go's 64-bit int, but would overflow a 32-bit one.
Save the speed when it works (best = m) and keep searching left. Returning at the first working speed gives a speed that is fast enough, not the smallest.

recap.key: Search the range of possible answers. A yes/no check that never flips back lets you drop half the range each time.
recap.complexity: Time O(n log m). Space O(1).
moves: Take the middle speed m and total ceil(pile / m) over all piles
Hours <= h: save m and go left. Otherwise go right
